title: The Speckled Monster
summary: Long ago, a sickness called smallpox travelled the world with sailors, soldiers and traders. It gave people a high fever and a bumpy rash, and many did not survive. But people noticed something amazing: anyone who got better almost never caught it again.

sections.heading: Meet the Speckled Monster
paragraphs: Imagine living in a town in the 1700s. Every few years, news spreads from house to house: the smallpox has come back. Shops close early. Families keep their children indoors. Church bells ring more often than usual. In England, people had a nickname for this disease that tells you how much they feared it. They called it the 'speckled monster'.

Where did the name come from? The word 'pox' is an old English word for a disease that causes pocks, the bumps or pits on the skin. In the 1500s, English speakers began calling this illness the 'small pox' to tell it apart from another disease of the time with larger sores, which people called the 'great pox'. So 'smallpox' did not mean a small illness. It referred to the size of the spots, not the size of the danger.

Smallpox was a disease caused by a virus called variola. A virus is a tiny particle, far too small to see even with an ordinary microscope, that can only make copies of itself inside living cells. Variola only infected humans. It had no animal hiding place and no insects to carry it, so it could survive only by jumping from one person to the next, again and again, for thousands of years.

The jump usually happened when people were close together, face to face. A sick person breathed out, coughed or spoke, and tiny droplets carrying the virus floated into the air. Someone nearby breathed them in. Less often, the virus spread through things a sick person had used, like bedding or clothing. That is why smallpox thrived in crowded towns, busy ports, army camps and ships, anywhere many people lived and worked side by side.

After someone caught the virus, nothing seemed to happen at first. For about one to two weeks the person felt completely normal while the virus quietly multiplied inside their body. Doctors call this hidden stretch the incubation period. Then the illness arrived suddenly: a high fever, a pounding headache, a sore back, aching muscles and a feeling of being terribly ill. This stage lasted two to four days.

Next came the part that gave smallpox its name. Small red spots appeared in the mouth and throat, and soon afterwards on the face. Over a day or so they spread to the arms, legs and body. The spots changed day by day in a regular pattern. First they became raised bumps. Then they filled with clear fluid, like tiny blisters. Then they filled with thicker, cloudy fluid and became firm, round bumps called pustules. After about two weeks the pustules dried into crusts, or scabs, which slowly fell off.

One thing doctors noticed was that the rash was usually thickest on the face, hands and feet, rather than on the chest and back. That pattern helped tell smallpox apart from chickenpox, a much milder illness whose spots cluster on the body instead.

A person with smallpox could pass it on from the moment the rash began until the very last scab dropped off, a period of roughly three weeks. That is why families and towns tried to keep the sick apart from everyone else, and why whole households could fall ill one after another.

Where the scabs had been, many survivors were left with small, pitted scars, especially on their faces. Between about two thirds and four fifths of survivors kept these marks for life. Some people also had damage to their eyes. In eighteenth-century Europe, smallpox is thought to have been the cause of about one third of all blindness.

sections.heading: Two Faces of One Disease: Major and Minor
paragraphs: Not all smallpox was equally dangerous. Doctors eventually realised that the variola virus came in two main forms, and the difference between them was enormous.

The first and more common form was called variola major. 'Major' means bigger or more serious, and the name fits. On average, about three in every ten people who caught variola major died. Children and older people were often hit hardest. The danger also depended on how thick the rash was. When the spots stayed separate, most people survived. When they ran together into large patches, the illness was far more likely to be deadly. A small number of cases took rarer, even more severe forms that almost nobody survived.

The second form was called variola minor, sometimes known by its older name, alastrim. It caused the same kind of fever and rash, but it was much gentler. Historically, about one person in a hundred, or fewer, died from it. Doctors only clearly recognised variola minor as a separate form around the end of the 1800s, and in the 1900s it became the main kind of smallpox in some places, including parts of the Americas and Africa.

Here is a fascinating twist: catching either form protected a person against the other. Someone who survived variola minor was safe from variola major, and the other way round. That tells us the two forms were close relatives, recognised by the body as almost the same enemy. Keep that idea in your pocket. Using a milder relative of a dangerous germ to protect against the deadly one will turn out to be one of the biggest ideas in this whole story.

It is worth pausing on what 'three in ten' really means. If smallpox swept through a village of 1,000 people who had never had it, and most of them caught it, several hundred might die within a few months. Almost every family would lose someone. That is why the arrival of smallpox felt like a disaster, not just an illness.

sections.heading: Clues in a Pharaoh's Face
paragraphs: How old is smallpox? Scientists who study the family tree of viruses think variola probably appeared somewhere between about 3,000 and 4,000 years ago. Its closest living relatives are two other pox viruses: camelpox, which infects camels, and taterapox, which was found in wild African rodents called gerbils. Many researchers suspect smallpox began when an ancient virus from animals learned to spread between people, but no one knows exactly where or when that happened.

For a long time, the most famous clue came from ancient Egypt. In 1898 the French archaeologist Victor Loret explored a hidden tomb in the Valley of the Kings near Luxor. Ancient priests had moved many royal mummies there for safekeeping, to protect them from tomb robbers. Among them was the mummy of Pharaoh Ramses V, a king who ruled for only about four years and died around 1145 BCE, while he was probably still in his early thirties.

In 1905 the anatomist Grafton Elliot Smith unwrapped and examined the mummy. He noticed something unusual: the pharaoh's face, neck and other parts of his body were covered in small, raised bumps. Later researchers compared them with smallpox pustules. Today you can see Ramses V at the National Museum of Egyptian Civilization in Cairo.

So did Ramses V die of smallpox? The honest answer is that we do not know. The bumps look like they could be smallpox scars or pustules, and many books describe him as one of the earliest possible victims. But no one has proven it, for example by finding the virus's genetic material in his body. Some researchers have even suggested other illnesses, such as plague, could explain the marks on his body. So the careful way to say it is that Ramses V may have had smallpox. Ancient Egyptian records also tell us that his burial was strangely delayed, but they do not tell us what killed him.

The strongest proof of smallpox's age came not from Egypt but from northern Europe, and it came from teeth. Teeth are excellent time capsules. When a person is ill, viruses travelling in the blood can leave traces of their genetic material inside the tooth, where it may survive for centuries.

In July 2020, a large team led by Eske Willerslev, working at the University of Cambridge and the University of Copenhagen, published a study in the journal Science. They had searched the remains of people buried during the Viking Age and earlier, at sites in places such as Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Russia and the United Kingdom. In the teeth of several skeletons they found the DNA of the variola virus. These were the oldest confirmed traces of smallpox ever discovered, about 1,400 years old. The team even rebuilt nearly complete genetic codes for four of the ancient viruses.

The results held a surprise. The Viking-age smallpox was a different strain from the one that was later wiped out in the 1900s. It belonged to a separate branch of the family that has since died out. Scientists still do not know whether that ancient strain was as deadly as the later one. One of the study's senior authors, Terry Jones, said that finding smallpox 'so genetically different in Vikings is truly remarkable.' The discovery reminds us that viruses change over time, and that the smallpox of history was not one unchanging thing.

sections.heading: Hitching a Ride with Traders and Armies
paragraphs: A virus that can only live inside people needs a steady supply of new people to infect. In a small, isolated village, smallpox would burn through everyone who could catch it and then vanish, because survivors could not catch it again. But in big, crowded places with lots of births and lots of visitors, there were always new children and newcomers who had never had it. As cities grew and trade routes linked them together, smallpox found a permanent home in human history.

Ancient writers described terrible epidemics, and historians still argue about which ones were smallpox. A great sickness that struck Athens in 430 BCE might have been smallpox, though it could have been something else. The Antonine Plague, which swept through the Roman Empire from about 165 to 180 CE after soldiers returned from wars in the east, is thought by many historians to have been smallpox. Estimates of its death toll run into the millions, though nobody counted carefully at the time.

Written descriptions that clearly match smallpox appear in China by the 300s CE and in India in medical writings from the early centuries CE. In India, people came to link the disease with a goddess named Sitala, who was believed to both bring and cool the fever. In 581 CE, a bishop in France named Gregory of Tours wrote an eyewitness account of an epidemic that sounds very much like smallpox.

Around the year 910, a brilliant Persian doctor named al-Razi, known in Europe as Rhazes, wrote a famous book about smallpox and measles. He described how the two illnesses looked and behaved, and he is often credited as the first doctor to clearly tell them apart. His book was copied and translated for hundreds of years.

Smallpox also reached islands that had been isolated for a long time. In Japan, an epidemic between 735 and 737 CE is believed to have killed a huge share of the population, possibly as much as a third. When a disease arrives in a place where nobody has met it before, everybody is vulnerable at once, adults as well as children.

Big historical movements helped too. The rapid expansion of Arab armies and traders from the 600s onwards linked North Africa, the Middle East and Spain. Later, the Crusades, a series of wars fought between Christian European armies and Muslim states from 1096 onwards, sent tens of thousands of soldiers and pilgrims back and forth between Europe and the eastern Mediterranean. Every one of these great movements of people was also a highway for germs, and historians think smallpox travelled along with them.

Over the following centuries, armies, pilgrims and merchants carried the virus along every road and sea lane. Wars moved crowds of soldiers. Trade caravans crossed deserts. Ships connected ports from the Mediterranean to the Indian Ocean. Each journey was a chance for the virus to travel to a new town. By the 1500s, smallpox was found across most of Asia, Europe and Africa. It had become what doctors call endemic: always present, flaring into epidemics every few years whenever enough unprotected children had been born.

sections.heading: A New World with No Defences
paragraphs: For thousands of years, the peoples of North and South America lived separately from Europe, Asia and Africa. Many Old World diseases, including smallpox, measles and influenza, had never crossed the ocean. That meant that when Europeans began arriving after Christopher Columbus's voyage in 1492, the people of the Americas had never been exposed to these germs. Nobody had survived them before, so nobody was protected. Historians sometimes call outbreaks like this 'virgin soil' epidemics, because the disease is landing on ground where it has never been.

Smallpox was first recorded in the Americas in 1518, in the Caribbean. From there it travelled to the mainland. In 1520 it reached Mexico with Spanish expeditions. At that time Tenochtitlan, the island capital of the Aztec (Mexica) Empire, was one of the largest cities in the world, with perhaps 200,000 people. While the Aztecs were fighting the Spanish soldiers led by Hernán Cortés, smallpox swept through the city. Historians estimate that about four in ten of its people died. Among those who died was the Aztec ruler Cuitláhuac, who had led the resistance against the Spanish. He died after only about 80 days in power, probably of smallpox, although the earliest records do not say for certain.

The disease moved faster than the soldiers. Smallpox, or a disease very like it, seems to have spread south and reached the Inca Empire in the Andes mountains before Francisco Pizarro's expedition arrived. The Inca emperor Huayna Capac and his chosen heir died during an epidemic in the 1520s. Their deaths helped trigger a civil war between two of his other sons, leaving the empire divided when the Spanish came.

The transatlantic slave trade also carried smallpox across the ocean. Millions of African people were forced onto crowded ships and taken to the Americas in terrible conditions. Some of them came from regions where smallpox was common, and outbreaks broke out on board and in the ports where the ships arrived. The cruelty of that trade and the spread of disease were bound together, and both caused enormous suffering.

Smallpox was not the only killer. Measles, influenza, typhus and other diseases arrived too, along with war, forced labour and the destruction of farms and communities. Together, these disasters caused one of the largest population collapses in human history. Historians estimate that a very large share of the Indigenous population of the Americas, possibly as much as 80 to 95 percent in some regions, died within about 100 to 150 years after 1492. The exact numbers are debated, because nobody knows for sure how many people lived in the Americas before 1492, but there is no doubt that the loss was enormous.

Further north, smallpox struck again and again. Epidemics swept through Indigenous communities in New England in the 1600s, and another great epidemic spread across much of North America between 1775 and 1782. Each time, whole villages lost elders, parents and children, along with knowledge, languages and traditions. When historians talk about how smallpox changed the world, the Americas are where its effects were most devastating.

sections.heading: Queens, Kings and a Young George Washington
paragraphs: Smallpox did not care whether you were a farmer or a king. In eighteenth-century Europe, it is estimated to have killed around 400,000 people every year. That is roughly like losing the whole population of a large city, every single year. It killed several reigning monarchs during that century, along with princes, princesses and heirs to thrones.

Some royal deaths changed history. Tsar Peter II of Russia died of smallpox in January 1730, aged just 14, on the very day that had been set for his wedding. King Louis XV of France died of it in 1774, aged 64, even though he had reigned for almost 60 years. Earlier, in 1694, Queen Mary II of England had died of smallpox in her early thirties. Each royal death could set off a scramble over who would rule next.

Some famous people survived. In October 1562, Queen Elizabeth I of England, then 29 years old, fell dangerously ill with smallpox at Hampton Court Palace near London. For several days her advisers feared she would die, and they began arguing about who should take the throne, since she had no children. She recovered. One of her ladies, Mary Sidney, nursed her through the illness, caught smallpox herself and was left badly scarred. The queen's close call made Parliament even more anxious that she should marry or name an heir.

Two centuries later, a young musician also had a narrow escape. In 1767, an 11-year-old boy named Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart caught smallpox while his family was travelling and staying in the city of Olomouc, in what is now the Czech Republic. He was ill for days, and according to family accounts his eyes were affected for a time, but he recovered and went on to write some of the most famous music ever composed.

Across the Atlantic, another young man caught smallpox on his only trip outside mainland North America. In 1751, 19-year-old George Washington sailed to the island of Barbados in the Caribbean with his older half-brother Lawrence, who was suffering from tuberculosis and hoped the warm climate would help him. In Barbados, George caught smallpox. He spent weeks recovering, and the disease left faint scars on his face for the rest of his life.

That illness turned out to matter. Because he had survived smallpox, Washington could no longer catch it. Years later, when he became commander of the American army during the Revolutionary War, he could walk among sick soldiers without fear for himself, and he understood exactly how dangerous the disease could be to an army. You will see what he did about that later in this story.

sections.heading: The Clue Everyone Noticed
paragraphs: Across thousands of years and many cultures, people noticed the same remarkable fact: if you survived smallpox once, you almost never caught it again. The disease that had tried to kill you seemed to leave behind an invisible shield.

This idea was not new even in ancient times. When the Greek historian Thucydides described the great sickness in Athens in 430 BCE, he noted that people who had recovered could care for the sick without danger, because the illness did not attack the same person twice, at least not fatally. Whether that disease was smallpox or something else, the observation was the same one people kept making.

In many places this knowledge shaped everyday life. Families often chose people who had already survived smallpox to nurse the sick, because they could do it safely. In Europe, servants who had already had smallpox were sometimes preferred by employers, and advertisements for jobs occasionally mentioned it. In some communities, a face marked with smallpox scars was almost like a badge that said: this person cannot catch it again.

People also noticed a second pattern. In big cities where smallpox came back every few years, most adults had already had it as children. So in places like London, smallpox was mainly thought of as a children's disease, and parents waited anxiously to see whether each child would survive it. In remote places where the virus arrived only rarely, it struck people of every age at once, which made those outbreaks even more frightening.

Nobody at the time understood why this happened. They did not know about viruses, or white blood cells, or the immune system, the body's defence network of cells, tissues and proteins that fights germs. Today we know that after a serious infection, the immune system keeps a kind of memory of the invader and can recognise it instantly the next time. But for most of history, people only saw the result, not the reason.

Meanwhile, smallpox kept killing. Even in the 20th century, long after people had learned how to fight it, the disease is estimated to have killed about 300 million people around the world. In the early 1950s there were still around 50 million cases each year. Very few diseases in human history have caused so much suffering.

Yet that one simple clue, that surviving smallpox protects you, contained the seed of a solution. Healers in different parts of the world began to think about it in a daring new way. If surviving a case of smallpox gives you lifelong protection, what if you could choose when and how you caught it? What if you could catch a smaller, gentler case, at a time when you were healthy and well cared for, and come out the other side protected forever? Could people give themselves a mild case of smallpox on purpose?

deepDive: How do we know what smallpox did in the past when the virus is now gone? Historians and scientists use several kinds of evidence, and each has limits. Written records are the oldest tool, but ancient writers did not use modern disease names, and smallpox, measles and chickenpox could be confused until physicians such as al-Razi described their differences around 910 CE. That is why historians still argue about whether the Plague of Athens (430 BCE) or the Antonine Plague (about 165 to 180 CE) were smallpox. Physical evidence such as the bumps on the mummy of Ramses V is suggestive but not proof, because other diseases can leave similar marks, and the mummy has never yielded variola DNA. The newest evidence comes from ancient DNA. In 2020, researchers led by Eske Willerslev and including Barbara Mühlemann and Terry Jones reported variola DNA in Viking-age and earlier remains from northern Europe, about 1,400 years old, and reconstructed four near-complete genomes. Those ancient viruses belonged to an extinct branch of the variola family, showing that smallpox evolved over time; some researchers think the later, highly deadly form may have spread more recently than once assumed. Molecular-clock studies, which estimate when viruses split apart by counting genetic differences, had earlier suggested a younger age for the modern virus, and the debate over smallpox's origins is far from settled. Numbers are another challenge. Estimates such as about 400,000 European deaths a year in the 1700s, or about 300 million deaths in the 20th century, come from incomplete records and careful modelling, so you will see ranges (for example 250 to 500 million) in different sources. Similarly, estimates of how many Indigenous Americans died after 1492 depend on how many people lived there beforehand, a figure historians still dispute. What no serious historian doubts is the overall pattern: variola major killed about 30 percent of those it infected, it shaped empires and families for centuries, and survivors gained lasting immunity. That last fact, recorded independently in many cultures, became the starting point for the first deliberate attempts to prevent the disease.
funFact: Scientists found the oldest confirmed smallpox DNA not in a pharaoh's tomb but inside the teeth of Viking-age skeletons, about 1,400 years old.

check.q: What did people all over the world notice about people who survived smallpox?
